title: Significance, change and writing like a historian

review.note: Built from Mr Garry's own lessons for this unit (2026–27 scheme of work). Check wording against the lesson PowerPoints before relying on it.

learn.intro: Who decides what deserves to be remembered? Does history always move forwards? And how do you turn all of this into a convincing argument? This topic finishes the unit with significance, change and continuity, and the Arcadia way of writing like a historian.

sections.title: 1. Historical significance

blocks.p: Important is not the same as historically significant. Historians judge significance using criteria, not personal preference:

ul: Scale: how many people were affected?
Impact: how much changed because of it?
Duration: how long did the effects last?
Revealing: what does it tell us about the time?
Remembered: how and why is it remembered today?

blocks.p: Significance can change over time, and something can be highly significant to one group and less so to another. Use "highly significant / somewhat significant / less significant" and then explain why.

evidence: Criteria: scale, impact, duration, revealing, remembered.

blocks.p: Change is something becoming different over time; continuity is something staying the same. Change can be rapid or gradual. A turning point is a moment after which things changed significantly.

Change is not always progress (change for the better). It can be decline (change for the worse), or progress for one group and decline for another. Dubai shows rapid change after oil was discovered in 1966, the UAE was formed in 1971 and new infrastructure was built, alongside continuities such as heritage, language and family traditions.
Time connectives plus explaining connectives help you explain change: Firstly… Then… As a result… This meant that… Therefore…

sections.title: 3. Writing like a historian: the Arcadia paragraph

blocks.p: A strong historical paragraph is not just a list of facts. It is an argument. The Arcadia model uses four moves, which match PEEJ:

ul: P: a qualified claim (QUALIFIER: highly / partly / to some extent).
E: precisely selected evidence (a name, date, number or source).
E: explanation with an explaining connective (because / this meant that / therefore) and time connectives where sequence matters.
J: a judgement that answers the question.

blocks.p: Ask yourself: What is my argument? How strongly do I want to claim it? Which evidence best proves it? How do I explain the link?

misconceptions.wrong: Significant just means "I think it is important".
misconceptions.right: Significance is judged against criteria such as scale, impact and duration.
Change can be decline, or progress for some and decline for others.

misconceptions.wrong: More facts make a better paragraph.
misconceptions.right: A paragraph full of facts can still be a poor argument. Facts must be selected and explained.
What people think is significant can change over time.

evidence.q: Use at least two criteria to explain why the discovery of oil in 1966 was significant for Dubai.
evidence.model: The discovery of oil in 1966 was highly significant. Its impact was huge because oil money paid for roads, ports and housing. Its duration is long because that infrastructure still shapes Dubai today.

evidence.q: Give one example of change and one of continuity in Dubai since 1966.
evidence.model: Change: the city grew rapidly, with new infrastructure such as the Dubai World Trade Centre (1979). Continuity: heritage and traditions, such as Arabic language and family customs, remained important.

exam.criteria_note: Practice questions written for this unit. AI feedback is formative only (no marks) until department KS3 criteria are added.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Which was more significant for Dubai: the discovery of oil in 1966 or the formation of the UAE in 1971? Write one Arcadia (PEEJ) paragraph.
questions.asks: Make a qualified judgement between the two, using significance criteria and precise evidence.
steps: Choose your best piece of evidence.
Explain using a criterion and a connective.
End with a judgement that compares both.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking for the four moves.

model.t: The discovery of oil in 1966 was arguably more significant for Dubai than the formation of the UAE, to a large extent because of its economic impact.
Oil revenue paid for new infrastructure, which helped projects such as the Dubai World Trade Centre, opened in 1979.
This meant Dubai could grow far faster than before, and as a result it became a centre of trade and travel.
However, the formation of the UAE in 1971 gave Dubai security and unity, so overall oil was more significant for growth, while 1971 was more significant politically.

full: P: … was highly / somewhat more significant than … because…
E: This meant that… As a result… Therefore…
J: Overall, … was more significant because…

questions.q: "History isn't simply a story of progress." Explain this statement using an example of change in Dubai.
questions.asks: Show that change can be progress, decline or both, depending on who is affected.
steps: Explain how it was progress for one group.
Explain how it might be decline or loss for another, or what stayed the same.
